title: Wildlife Observer's Field Journal
subtitle: A saga about discovering inheritance
completeMessage: You have discovered the core patterns of Object-Oriented Inheritance.

acts.name: The Pattern

transferScenario.title: A New Field List
transferScenario.text: Priya opens a second page in her journal. This time she is watching three vehicles on the road: a Bicycle, a Car, and a Truck. They look completely different on the outside, but Priya notices every one of them has wheels, carries people or goods, and needs energy to move.
transferScenario.question: Now, using your understanding: what do the Bicycle, the Car, and the Truck all share? What single label would you group them under?
options: Nothing, they are completely unrelated
They all have wheels, carry people or goods, and need energy, so group them under Vehicles
They are all vehicles, but they share no common traits
transferScenario.hint: Look for the shared needs every one of them has: wheels, carrying things, and energy.

narrative.speaker: narrator
narrative.text: Dawn breaks over Vedanta Reserve. Dr. Priya studies three animals — a lion, an eagle, and a dolphin.

narrative.speaker: priya
narrative.text: Three completely different animals. Let's see if there's a pattern hiding between them, Pip.

narrative.speaker: lion
narrative.text: ROAR! I breathe every moment. I hunt, I move, I eat. Every. Single. Day.

narrative.speaker: eagle
narrative.text: Same here! I breathe too. I soar to move, I hunt to eat — every single day without fail!

narrative.speaker: dolphin
narrative.text: Me too! I breathe, I swim, I eat fish. We all do the exact same things!

narrative.speaker: priya
narrative.text: Despite looking so different — they share the exact same core behaviours. We should group them under one single label.

acts.observationPrompt: Dr. Priya turns to you and taps her journal.
questions: What do all three animals have in common?
Since they share these traits, we can group them together under one label (like 'Animal' or 'Living Thing'). What label would you give them?
acts.expectedInsight: Learner identifies shared/common traits across all animals, generalization thinking, recognizing a base pattern
summaryGuide: Several different things can share the same core traits.
When they do, we group them under one shared label.
In Python, that label becomes a class, the foundation every member builds on.

storyBridge.speaker: priya
storyBridge.text: You found the shared traits, breathe, move, eat. Every animal has them. Now here is something interesting.

storyBridge.speaker: pip
storyBridge.text: Hoo! Programmers face the exact same problem, how to group things that share common traits! They solved it the same way you did!

storyBridge.speaker: priya
storyBridge.text: In programming, a group of shared traits is called a class. The word class means exactly what you just described. Let me show you how to write it.

syntaxLesson.storyConnection: "Every single one of them breathes. Every one of them moves. And every one of them eats.", Dr. Priya
syntaxLesson.explanation: Just like Dr. Priya opened her notebook and wrote the heading 'Animal' to group the lion, eagle, and dolphin, programmers use the keyword 'class' to create a group. 'class Animal:' is the heading of our digital notebook.
syntaxLesson.code:
class Animal:
    pass  # shared traits go inside here

syntaxLesson.storyConnection: Priya's journal lists three traits every animal has: breathe, move, eat.
syntaxLesson.explanation: Dr. Priya noticed they all breathe, move, and eat. In Python, we define these shared actions using 'def' (short for define). Inside our Animal class, we define breathe, move, and eat so every animal in this group automatically knows how to do them.

syntaxLesson.storyConnection: Any animal Priya observes, lion, eagle, dolphin, gets all the shared traits automatically.
syntaxLesson.explanation: Because we defined those actions in the Animal class, the moment we spot a lion and tell Python it is an Animal, it automatically knows how to breathe, move, and eat. The shared pattern works!
syntaxLesson.code:
lion = Animal()
lion.breathe() # breathing...
lion.move() # moving...
lion.eat() # eating...

observationOptions.question: What do the Lion, Eagle, and Dolphin all have in common?
options: They all live in the same habitat
They all breathe, move around, and eat
They all have the same shape and size
observationOptions.hint: Priya noticed shared behaviours, not appearances. What actions does every single one of them do every day?

mcqs.question: If we group the Lion, Eagle, and Dolphin into one category based on their shared traits, what concept are we applying?
options: Specialization
Generalization
Randomization
mcqs.hint: Think about finding the 'general' pattern that applies to all of them.

mcqs.question: Which label best groups objects that share the same core traits?
options: Specialization
Generalization
Randomization
mcqs.hint: Think about grouping by shared features, not splitting apart.

mcqs.question: The lion, the eagle, and the dolphin share the same core traits. What is the smartest way to record them?
options: Write the same traits three times, once per animal
Record the shared traits once under one group label
Give each animal completely different traits
mcqs.hint: Why write the same behaviour down three times when one group can hold it?

acts.name: The Eagle's Secret

transferScenario.title: The Racing Car
transferScenario.text: Back at the workshop, Priya looks at her vehicle notes again. The Racing Car has wheels, carries people, and needs energy, exactly like every vehicle. But it also has a nitro boost that no other vehicle on the list has.
transferScenario.question: Using your understanding, how does the Racing Car build on top of the shared vehicle pattern? What does it keep, and what does it add?
options: It keeps nothing from the shared vehicle pattern
It keeps wheels, carrying, and energy, and adds a nitro boost
It replaces the vehicle pattern completely
transferScenario.hint: The racing car is still a vehicle first, then it adds something special.

narrative.speaker: narrator
narrative.text: The next morning. Priya focuses her binoculars on the eagle on its high branch.

narrative.speaker: eagle
narrative.text: I breathe and eat like all animals, but watch THIS!

narrative.speaker: narrator
narrative.text: The eagle stretches its wings and launches, soaring effortlessly above the canopy.

narrative.speaker: priya
narrative.text: It flies! It belongs to the Animal group so it has all the foundation — but it ALSO has this specific ability entirely its own.

narrative.speaker: pip
narrative.text: Hoo! We need a way to say: 'it gets everything from the base group, PLUS this extra thing'!

acts.observationPrompt: Priya circles the eagle in her journal.
questions: What does the eagle share with every other animal?
What can the eagle do that the others can't?
How would you describe the eagle's place in the animal group?
acts.expectedInsight: Learner articulates the extension relationship: eagle = shared animal foundation + something uniquely its own (is-a pattern with specialization)
summaryGuide: A child keeps every trait of the shared group automatically.
Then it adds its own special ability on top.
In Python, class Eagle(Animal): says “Eagle IS-A Animal”.

storyBridge.speaker: priya
storyBridge.text: Excellent. The eagle IS an animal, it has the full foundation. And it can fly, that extra ability is its own.

storyBridge.speaker: pip
storyBridge.text: Hoo! Programmers call this a child class! Eagle is the child. Animal is the parent. Child gets everything from parent!

storyBridge.speaker: priya
storyBridge.text: In Python, we write this with just one small thing, Animal in parentheses. That one addition connects Eagle to everything it inherits. Watch.

syntaxLesson.storyConnection: "The eagle has everything a general animal has... and then something that belongs only to it.", Dr. Priya
syntaxLesson.explanation: Dr. Priya observed that the eagle has everything an animal has. In Python, we put '(Animal)' right next to 'Eagle' to tell the program exactly what Priya saw: The Eagle is a child of the Animal group, and inherits all its traits.

syntaxLesson.storyConnection: "It flies. The lion doesn't. The dolphin doesn't.", Dr. Priya
syntaxLesson.explanation: Priya didn't write down 'breathes' again for the eagle, she only wrote what makes it special. Python does the same. Inside the Eagle class, we only define 'fly()'. It gets breathe, move, and eat automatically.
syntaxLesson.code:
class Eagle(Animal):
    def fly(self):
        print("soaring high!")

# Eagle gets from Animal, for free:
# breathe(), move(), eat()
# Eagle adds its own:
# fly()

syntaxLesson.slideTitle: Step 3, Eagle Gets Animal's Traits for Free
syntaxLesson.storyConnection: The eagle never had to learn to breathe, it got that from the Animal group automatically.
syntaxLesson.explanation: Just as the eagle naturally knows how to breathe without learning it, our Python eagle object can use 'eagle.breathe()' even though we only wrote 'fly()'. It inherited the basic traits from the Animal class.
syntaxLesson.code:
eagle = Eagle()
eagle.breathe() # from Animal ← inherited!
eagle.move() # from Animal ← inherited!
eagle.fly() # Eagle's own ← defined here

observationOptions.question: How is the eagle related to the Animal group?
options: It is completely different from every animal
It shares all the animal traits and adds flying
It only has its flying ability and nothing else
observationOptions.hint: Look at both parts of the eagle entry: the shared foundation AND the unique ability.

mcqs.question: Because the Eagle shares all traits of an Animal but adds flying, we can say that the Eagle...
options: is NOT an Animal.
is a specialization of an Animal.
replaces the Animal entirely.
mcqs.hint: The eagle builds on top of the Animal foundation. It's a specific type of Animal.

mcqs.question: What does the eagle get from the Animal group automatically?
options: The ability to fly
Breathing, moving, and eating
A new habitat
mcqs.hint: The things every single animal can do.

mcqs.question: Saying the eagle is a specialized Animal means...
options: The eagle is an Animal plus something extra
The eagle is not an Animal at all
The eagle only flies and has nothing else
mcqs.hint: Think about the eagle two parts: the shared foundation and its own ability.

acts.name: The Word

transferScenario.title: Phone and Smartphone
transferScenario.text: The next day, Priya finds a simpler example in her pocket. Her old Mobile phone can call, message, and play music. Her new Smartphone can do ALL of that too, and it also has a touchscreen.
transferScenario.question: The Mobile does everything, and the Smartphone does that PLUS adds a touchscreen. What do we call this pattern, in your own words?
options: It is called skipping, the phone skips its old features
It is inheritance: the smartphone gets everything from the phone and adds its own touchscreen
It is copying: the smartphone copies exactly the same features with nothing new
transferScenario.hint: The pattern got its official name when you used it on a phone pair.

narrative.speaker: priya
narrative.text: You've described something important — the eagle gets everything from the Animal group automatically, then adds its own ability on top.

narrative.speaker: eagle
narrative.text: So I inherit all my animal traits automatically, but my soaring is all mine?

narrative.speaker: narrator
narrative.text: Priya writes a single word in large letters across the page.

narrative.speaker: priya
narrative.text: When one type automatically receives all the traits of another and adds its own — we call this: INHERITANCE.

acts.observationPrompt: The word hangs in the air. Priya looks at you.
questions: Can you think of something from real life that works the same way, belongs to a group, but also has something extra of its own?
acts.expectedInsight: Learner can transfer the pattern to a new domain, showing they understand the concept, not just memorized the story
summaryGuide: When one type automatically receives all the traits of another and adds its own, it is called Inheritance.
Animal is the parent, Eagle is the child.
Parent = shared foundation. Child = foundation + its own additions.

storyBridge.speaker: priya
storyBridge.text: You found your own example of inheritance. That means you genuinely understand the pattern, not just the story.

storyBridge.speaker: pip
storyBridge.text: Hoo! Now let's see the full Python picture, with all the right vocabulary!

storyBridge.speaker: priya
storyBridge.text: Parent class. Child class. Inherit. These are the exact words Python uses for everything you have been describing. Let me show you all of it together.

syntaxLesson.storyConnection: Animal is the general group. Eagle is the specific type that builds on it.
syntaxLesson.explanation: The story called this a general group and a specific member. Python uses family names. 'Animal' is the Parent class holding the foundation. 'Eagle' is the Child class that inherits the foundation.

syntaxLesson.storyConnection: "When one type automatically receives all the traits of another, we call this Inheritance.", Dr. Priya
syntaxLesson.explanation: When you read 'class Eagle(Animal):', imagine Dr. Priya drawing an arrow from the Eagle to the Animal group. The parentheses mean 'I inherit from this'. The child gets the parent's traits, and adds its own.
syntaxLesson.code:
class Eagle(Animal):
# ^ ^
# child parent
#
# Eagle inherits: breathe(), move(), eat()
# Eagle adds own: fly()

syntaxLesson.storyConnection: You already understood this from the story. The code just writes it down.
syntaxLesson.explanation: This is the full translation of Dr. Priya's journal into code. The parent class defines the common ground, and the child class inherits it and adds its unique abilities. Look closely at how they connect.

observationOptions.question: Pick the real-world pair that matches the pattern from the story.
options: A book and a library shelf
A smartphone, which is a phone with an added touchscreen
A lamp and a light bulb
observationOptions.hint: One thing must inherit everything from another type, then add its own new thing.

mcqs.question: Which of the following is the best real-world example of Inheritance?
options: A steering wheel being part of a Car.
A Smartphone inheriting from a general Phone, but adding a touchscreen.
A Dog chasing a Cat.
mcqs.hint: Look for a relationship where one thing IS A type of another thing, just with more features.

mcqs.question: Animal is the parent and Eagle is the child. Which phrase best describes their relationship?
options: They are the same thing
The child receives the parent traits and adds its own
The child throws away the parent traits
mcqs.hint: Remember the family vocabulary.

mcqs.question: When one type automatically receives all the traits of another and adds its own, what is this called?
options: Inheritance
Assembly
Isolation
mcqs.hint: The single word written in large letters across the page.

acts.name: First Code

narrative.speaker: priya
narrative.text: Now let's see how Python says what you already understand. Look at this, Animal exists as a class. The eagle inherits from it.

narrative.speaker: eagle
narrative.text: Finally! Time to put my soaring ability into the code!

narrative.speaker: pip
narrative.text: Hoo! It's time to write the code!

acts.expectedInsight: Learner fills class Eagle(Animal):, mapping their story understanding to Python syntax

storyBridge.speaker: priya
storyBridge.text: You've done it. You saw that lion, eagle, dolphin all breathe, move, and eat, and the eagle builds on top of that foundation with flying. Now let me show you something remarkable.

storyBridge.speaker: pip
storyBridge.text: Hoo! Programmers noticed this exact same pattern long before you picked up this journal, Doctor!

storyBridge.speaker: priya
storyBridge.text: In Python, a group of shared traits is called a class. And when one type extends another, like Eagle extends Animal, Python has a precise way of writing that relationship. Let's build it together, piece by piece.

syntaxLesson.storyConnection: "Every single one of them breathes. Every one of them moves. And every one of them eats.", Dr. Priya
syntaxLesson.explanation: We start exactly how Priya started her journal, by defining the general Animal group. This class acts as the foundation that every animal will build upon.

syntaxLesson.storyConnection: "The eagle has everything a general animal has... and then something that belongs only to it.", Dr. Priya
syntaxLesson.explanation: By putting '(Animal)' after Eagle, we tell Python what Priya saw: The Eagle is an Animal, and it gets all those foundational traits automatically without rewriting them.

syntaxLesson.storyConnection: "The eagle never had to learn to breathe, it got that from the Animal group automatically."
syntaxLesson.explanation: Even though we never wrote a breathe action inside the Eagle class, Python checks the Animal parent class and finds it there. The eagle inherited it perfectly.
syntaxLesson.code:
eagle = Eagle()
eagle.breathe() # inherited from Animal ✓
eagle.move() # inherited from Animal ✓
eagle.fly() # Eagle's own ability ✓

blanks.hint: What group does the Eagle get its shared traits from?

codeReveal.explanation: class Eagle(Animal): tells Python that Eagle is a specialization of Animal. Eagle automatically gets breathe(), move(), and eat(), just like you described.

summaryGuide: class Eagle(Animal): means Eagle is a specialization of Animal.
The parent class holds the shared traits.
The eagle automatically gets everything Animal defines, and adds its own fly().

codeTask.title: Now Try, You Write the Code
codeTask.instructions: Write the complete file yourself: define the Animal class with breathe(), move(), and eat(); then define class Eagle(Animal) with fly(); then create an eagle object and call eagle.breathe() and eagle.fly() like in the slides.

mcqs.question: In the relationship between Animal and Eagle, which one is considered the 'Parent' class?
options: Eagle
Animal
Both are Parents
mcqs.hint: The Parent class is the general one that passes its traits down.

mcqs.question: Which line of code makes the Eagle inherit from Animal?
options: class Eagle(Animal):
class Animal(Eagle):
eagle = Animal()
mcqs.hint: Look at the parentheses right after the class name.

mcqs.question: After class Eagle(Animal):, can the eagle object use eagle.breathe()?
options: No, that method is lost
Yes, it inherited breathe() from Animal
Only if we rewrite breathe() inside Eagle
mcqs.hint: Inheritance sends the traits down automatically.

acts.name: The Copycat Problem

transferScenario.title: The Penguin's Move
transferScenario.text: Priya watches a penguin at the new exhibit. Penguins are birds, they all have beaks and feathers. But a penguin cannot fly through the air. Instead of flying, it swims through the water, gliding fast with its flippers.
transferScenario.question: The penguin's “move” behaviour looks different from a normal bird. Is the penguin inventing a brand new behaviour, or doing the bird behaviour in its own unique way?
options: A brand new behaviour invented by the penguin
The bird behaviour done in the penguin own unique way
The penguin stops being a bird
transferScenario.hint: The penguin is still doing the move behaviour, just differently.

narrative.speaker: narrator
narrative.text: A week later. Priya watches a chameleon hunt near the river's edge. Every animal eats — she knows that from Act 1.

narrative.speaker: chameleon
narrative.text: You think I eat like a normal animal? Open, chew, swallow? Boring. Watch this.

narrative.speaker: narrator
narrative.text: The chameleon locks its eyes on a fly. In one lightning movement its tongue shoots out three times the length of its body, snatches the fly, and retracts. It never moved its feet.

narrative.speaker: priya
narrative.text: Wait. It belongs to the Animal group, so it should eat the normal way. But it just completely ignored the normal way!

narrative.speaker: pip
narrative.text: Hoo! It still eats, Doctor — it just does it in its OWN way! It replaced the group's default with something entirely its own!

acts.observationPrompt: Priya underlines 'eat' in her notes twice.
questions: Is the chameleon doing something brand new, or doing what every animal does, just in its own way?
What happens to the original way of eating when the chameleon does it differently? Does it disappear?
acts.expectedInsight: Learner understands that the chameleon replaces/specializes an inherited behaviour rather than adding something new, the concept of overriding without the word

storyBridge.speaker: priya
storyBridge.text: You saw it. The chameleon isn't inventing something new, eating already existed. It takes that inherited behaviour and replaces it with its own version.

storyBridge.speaker: pip
storyBridge.text: Hoo! Programmers call this overriding! When a child class does a parent's action in its own way, it overrides it!

storyBridge.speaker: priya
storyBridge.text: The key is: eating still works normally for the lion and the dolphin. Only the chameleon's version is different. Let me show you how Python writes this, step by step.

syntaxLesson.storyConnection: "Every animal eats. Open mouth, chew, swallow. That's the general pattern.", Dr. Priya
syntaxLesson.explanation: The Animal class already defines a basic 'eat' action. If the Chameleon just inherits this, it will eat like a standard animal, which Priya knows is wrong.

syntaxLesson.storyConnection: "Its tongue shoots out three times the length of its body... the chameleon never moved its feet.", Narrator
syntaxLesson.explanation: Priya noted the chameleon catches flies with its tongue. To tell Python to use this new way, we write 'def eat(self)' again inside the Chameleon class. Because it has the exact same name, it overrides the parent's version.

syntaxLesson.storyConnection: "The original still works for other animals, but the chameleon uses its own version."
syntaxLesson.explanation: The original animal eating method didn't disappear, lions and dolphins still use it. But when a Chameleon eats, Python sees its custom 'eat()' method and uses that instead. The chameleon overrode the default!
syntaxLesson.code:
c = Chameleon()
c.eat()  # → tongue-flick! (Chameleon's version)

a = Animal()
a.eat()  # → opens mouth and swallows (Animal's still works)

blanks.hint: The chameleon's eat() replaces the Animal's eat(). In programming, this is called ____ing.

codeReveal.explanation: When a child class defines a method with the same name as a parent's method, it overrides it. The child's version runs instead.

summaryGuide: The chameleon did not invent eating, it replaced the inherited way with its own version.
Same method name in the child, different behaviour = overriding.
The parent's version stays for everyone else.

codeTask.title: Now Try, You Write the Code
codeTask.instructions: Write the file yourself: class Animal with def eat(self) that prints the normal way, and class Chameleon(Animal) that overrides eat() with the tongue-flick version. Then create a chameleon and an animal, and call eat() on both to show each keeps its own version.

observationOptions.question: What is the chameleon really doing when it eats with its tongue?
options: Adding a completely new behaviour no animal has
Taking the existing eating behaviour and doing it in its own way
Forgetting how to eat
observationOptions.hint: Eating already existed. The chameleon only changed HOW it eats.

mcqs.question: When the Chameleon 'eats' differently than a normal Animal, what is it doing to the inherited behavior?
options: Deleting it from the parent.
Overriding it with its own custom version.
Ignoring it completely.
mcqs.hint: The original still exists for other animals, but the Chameleon chooses to use its own version.

mcqs.question: When the chameleon overrides eat(), what happens to the Animal version?
options: It disappears forever
It still works for other animals like the lion
It gets deleted from the class
mcqs.hint: Only the chameleon changed.

mcqs.question: How does Python know the chameleon has its own eat()?
options: Because the method has the same name as the parent inside the child class
Because the method has a random name
Because you must call something called override
mcqs.hint: Same name in the child means override.

acts.name: Whisper Back to the Elder

transferScenario.title: Grandma's Recipe
transferScenario.text: Priya writes down her grandmother's vada recipe. The base recipe says: “make the batter, then fry.” The family’s Special Vada does exactly those two steps first, and ONLY after that does it add its secret spice mix.
transferScenario.question: The Special Vada does the normal recipe first, then layers its own twist on top. Using your understanding, how is this different from replacing the recipe completely? What are the two steps, in order?
options: It replaces the recipe completely and forgets the base steps
It does the two base steps first, then adds the secret spice mix
It adds the spice first, then makes the batter
transferScenario.hint: Order matters: the base first, then the twist.

narrative.speaker: narrator
narrative.text: Priya rewinds the slow-motion tape of the chameleon. She thinks they missed something.

narrative.speaker: chameleon
narrative.text: Watch closely in slow motion. I don't completely ignore the old ways. I just add my own flair.

narrative.speaker: priya
narrative.text: Look closely at its jaw. Before the tongue shoots out... it still opens its mouth. That's the normal eating behaviour of the whole Animal group!

narrative.speaker: pip
narrative.text: Hoo! So it didn't throw away the normal way entirely! It does the normal thing FIRST, then adds its own twist on top!

narrative.speaker: priya
narrative.text: Exactly. Foundation first, then extension. It's the same pattern again — just applied to eating, not to the class definition.

acts.observationPrompt: Priya draws two steps in her journal.
questions: The chameleon opens its mouth first, then does the tongue-flick. How is that different from just replacing eating completely?
In your own words, describe the two steps the chameleon follows.
acts.expectedInsight: Learner describes the pattern: first do the inherited behaviour, then layer your own on top, the concept behind super() without the word

storyBridge.speaker: priya
storyBridge.text: You described it perfectly, first the foundation, then the twist. Two steps, in order. Not a replacement, an extension of what was inherited.

storyBridge.speaker: pip
storyBridge.text: Hoo! Python has a special tool for exactly this, it's called super(). It lets the child say: do the parent's version first, then I'll add my own!

storyBridge.speaker: priya
storyBridge.text: Think of super() as the chameleon whispering to its elder: 'I'll do what you do first, then I'll add my move.' Let me build it up step by step.

syntaxLesson.storyConnection: "Before the tongue-flick, it still opens its mouth. Like every animal does.", Dr. Priya
syntaxLesson.explanation: Priya noticed the chameleon still opens its mouth first, just like the elder animals. This basic action lives inside the parent Animal class.

syntaxLesson.slideTitle: Step 2, Call the Elder, Then Extend
syntaxLesson.storyConnection: "It reuses the foundation it inherited... then extends it.", Dr. Priya
syntaxLesson.explanation: In Python, 'super()' is how the chameleon whispers to its elder. 'super().eat()' tells Python to run the parent's normal eating action first. Then, on the next line, we add the chameleon's special tongue-flick.

syntaxLesson.storyConnection: "It does the normal thing first... then adds its twist on top."
syntaxLesson.explanation: When the chameleon eats now, Python follows the two steps Priya drew: first it opens its mouth (the inherited elder way), and THEN it shoots its tongue (the child's extension). Reuse before extending!
syntaxLesson.code:
c = Chameleon()
c.eat()
# Output:
# opens mouth... ← from Animal via super()
# ...THEN tongue-flick! ← Chameleon's own

blanks.hint: This Python keyword lets a child class 'call back' to its parent's version of a method.

codeReveal.explanation: super() is Python's way of saying 'call the parent class version of this method.' The chameleon uses super().eat() to run Animal's eat() first, then adds its own behaviour after, reuse before extend.

summaryGuide: super() is the child whispering to the parent: “do your version first.”
Then the child adds its own behaviour on top.
Reuse the inherited behaviour, then extend it.

codeTask.title: Now Try, You Write the Code
codeTask.instructions: Write the file yourself: class Animal with an eat() that prints “opens mouth...”, and class Chameleon(Animal) whose eat() calls super().eat() first and then prints the tongue-flick. Create a chameleon, call eat(), and show the two-line output.

observationOptions.question: How does the chameleon eat, from start to finish?
options: It only does the tongue-flick and skips everything else
It opens its mouth first, then does the tongue-flick
It never uses its mouth at all
observationOptions.hint: Two steps, in order: the normal mouth action first, then its own twist.

mcqs.question: Why does the Chameleon use a 'call back' to the elder's behavior?
options: To erase the parent's eating method.
To reuse the parent's normal eating method first, before adding its own twist.
To become a super animal.
mcqs.hint: It wants to keep the shared behavior, not throw it away.

mcqs.question: What does super() do in Python?
options: It deletes the parent method
It lets the child call the parent version of a method
It creates a brand new class
mcqs.hint: Think of whispering back to the elder.

mcqs.question: Why does the chameleon eat() run super().eat() first?
options: To reuse the normal eating behaviour before adding the tongue-flick
To make the program slower
To erase Animal eat()
mcqs.hint: Reuse before extend.

acts.name: Born Different

transferScenario.title: The Snow Leopard Entry
transferScenario.text: A rare snow leopard is found in the mountains. At the very moment it is discovered, Priya must log three things: its name, its habitat (like every animal), and its fur length (special to snow leopards).
transferScenario.question: In what order should the fields be filled in, and why? Which fields come from the shared animal record, and which are the snow leopard's own?
options: Fill name and habitat first from the shared animal record, then the fur length
Fill the fur length first, then name and habitat
Never fill the shared fields, only the special one
transferScenario.hint: Standard birth record first, special details after.

narrative.speaker: narrator
narrative.text: Back at the field station. Priya is logging each animal into her catalogue system.

narrative.speaker: priya
narrative.text: The very moment we discover any new animal, I always write two things first: name and habitat. It's the standard birth record for the group.

narrative.speaker: eagle
narrative.text: Hey! Don't forget my wingspan! I need that recorded immediately too!

narrative.speaker: narrator
narrative.text: Priya points to the eagle's log: Name, Habitat, and Wingspan — all recorded at the exact same moment it was discovered.

narrative.speaker: priya
narrative.text: The eagle needs the standard fields filled first, then its wingspan added right after. Foundation before extension — just like before.

acts.observationPrompt: Priya flips back to the eagle's first entry.
questions: The eagle needs name, habitat, and wingspan the moment it's recorded. Does this remind you of the pattern you already found?
Should the standard animal fields be filled in first, or the wingspan? Does the order matter?
acts.expectedInsight: Learner sees that even initialization follows the inheritance pattern, the child's constructor should handle the parent's required fields first, then its own additions

storyBridge.speaker: priya
storyBridge.text: You got it, the eagle's birth record needs the standard fields first, then its own. Foundation before extension. The exact same pattern, applied to the very moment an object comes into existence.

storyBridge.speaker: pip
storyBridge.text: Hoo! In Python, the 'birth record' is a special method called __init__. It runs the moment you create any object!

storyBridge.speaker: priya
storyBridge.text: And just like Act 6, the child's __init__ calls super() to set up the parent's fields first, before adding its own. Let me show you, layer by layer.

syntaxLesson.storyConnection: "Every animal I log gets a name and a habitat the moment I record it.", Dr. Priya
syntaxLesson.explanation: Priya noticed every single animal gets a name and habitat immediately when recorded. In Python, this 'birth record' is the __init__ method. The Animal class sets up these standard fields first.
syntaxLesson.code:
class Animal:
    def __init__(self, name, habitat):
        self.name = name
        self.habitat = habitat  # Every Animal needs name + habitat from the start


a = Animal("Leo", "savanna")
print(a.name)     # Leo
print(a.habitat)  # savanna

syntaxLesson.storyConnection: "The eagle needed an extra field right from the start, wingspan.", Dr. Priya
syntaxLesson.explanation: For the eagle, Priya needed to record wingspan right away. In Python, the Eagle's __init__ first calls super().__init__() to fill out the standard animal fields, and THEN adds the wingspan. Foundation first, then extension.

syntaxLesson.storyConnection: "Name, habitat, wingspan, all three recorded in the very first entry."
syntaxLesson.explanation: Now, the moment a new Eagle is created in the program, it instantly gets its name and habitat (from the parent's setup) AND its wingspan (from its own setup). All three fields are ready perfectly on time.
syntaxLesson.code:
e = Eagle("Eddie", "mountains", 2.1)
print(e.name) # Eddie ← from Animal
print(e.habitat) # mountains ← from Animal
print(e.wingspan) # 2.1 ← Eagle's own

blanks.hint: The same keyword from Act 6, call the parent's __init__ to handle the shared fields before adding your own.

codeReveal.explanation: super().__init__() calls Animal's constructor to set up the shared fields (name, habitat) before Eagle adds its own (wingspan). The pattern is exactly the same as Act 6, call the elder's setup first, then extend.

summaryGuide: The child's __init__ must set up the parent's fields first.
super().__init__() handles the shared “birth record.”
Then the child adds its own fields. Foundation first, then extension.

birth

acts.name: The Family Tree Grows

transferScenario.title: The Electric Car
transferScenario.text: Priya is reorganizing the vehicle catalogue: Vehicle → Car → ElectricCar. The ElectricCar has wheels and a frame (from Vehicle), has a steering wheel and seats (from Car, its parent), and adds a battery and charging port (its own).
transferScenario.question: Using your understanding of the family tree: what does the ElectricCar get from each level, Vehicle, the Car, and itself? Does it need to redefine wheels again? Why not?
options: It must redefine wheels again because each level is separate
It gets wheels and frame from Vehicle, steering and seats from Car, and adds a battery and charging port itself
It gets nothing from the whole chain
transferScenario.hint: One set of traits per level, everything flows down the chain.

narrative.speaker: narrator
narrative.text: Priya is organizing her catalogue and realizes her 'Animal' category is getting too broad.

narrative.speaker: priya
narrative.text: Birds have feathers, lay eggs, and have beaks. Not all animals have those... but all birds do. The eagle is really a specialized Bird, not just a direct specialization of Animal.

narrative.speaker: eagle
narrative.text: It's true! I'm a bird first and foremost. Then an eagle.

narrative.speaker: pip
narrative.text: Hoo! So the eagle inherits from Bird, and Bird inherits from Animal?

narrative.speaker: priya
narrative.text: Exactly. It's a chain. The eagle gets 'breathe' from Animal, 'feathers' from Bird, and adds 'sharp talons' itself.

questions: Why is it better to have Animal → Bird → Eagle instead of connecting Eagle directly to Animal?
Does Eagle need to redefine 'breathe'? Why or why not?
acts.expectedInsight: Learner understands multi-level inheritance: a child can inherit from a parent that itself is a child, automatically getting traits from all ancestors.

storyBridge.speaker: priya
storyBridge.text: You saw the power of the chain. Eagle and Sparrow both share bird-specific traits, write them once in Bird, and both get them automatically. No repetition.

storyBridge.speaker: pip
storyBridge.text: Hoo! And Python passes the baton down the entire chain, Animal to Bird to Eagle, automatically!

storyBridge.speaker: priya
storyBridge.text: Let me grow the family tree piece by piece in Python, starting from the very top and adding each layer, just like we'd sketch it in the field journal.

syntaxLesson.storyConnection: "Breathing, moving, eating, these are universal. Every creature in the reserve shares them.", Dr. Priya
syntaxLesson.explanation: Priya started her family tree at the very top: the Animal class. This holds universal traits like breathing that every single creature in the reserve shares.

syntaxLesson.storyConnection: "Birds have feathers, lay eggs, and have beaks. Not all animals have those, but all birds do.", Dr. Priya
syntaxLesson.explanation: Next, Priya added a middle layer. 'Bird' inherits all the universal Animal traits, but adds things specific to birds, like laying eggs. It's a child of Animal, but it's about to become a parent itself.

syntaxLesson.storyConnection: "The eagle is really a specialized Bird, not just a direct specialization of Animal.", Dr. Priya
syntaxLesson.explanation: Finally, Priya placed the Eagle at the bottom. By inheriting from Bird, the Eagle gets the bird traits (laying eggs), AND the chain automatically passes down the Animal traits (breathing) too. Everything flows down.

syntaxLesson.storyConnection: "The eagle gets 'breathe' from Animal, 'feathers' from Bird, and adds 'sharp talons' itself.", Dr. Priya
syntaxLesson.explanation: The eagle object now has access to three levels of history. It breathes from its grandparent (Animal), lays eggs from its parent (Bird), and soars using its own unique ability. The family tree is complete.
syntaxLesson.code:
e = Eagle()
e.breathe() # ← from Animal (2 levels up!)
e.lay_eggs() # ← from Bird (1 level up)
e.soar() # ← Eagle's own

blanks.hint: What does Bird inherit from in the chain?

codeReveal.explanation: In multi-level inheritance, a class inherits from another derived class. Eagle gets methods from both Bird and Animal automatically.

summaryGuide: In multi-level inheritance, traits flow down the whole chain.
Eagle inherits bird traits from Bird AND animal traits from Animal.
No repetition, write shared traits once, higher up.

codeTask.title: Now Try, You Write the Code
codeTask.instructions: Write the file yourself: class Animal with breathe(), class Bird(Animal) with lay_eggs(), and class Eagle(Bird) with soar(). Then create an eagle and call breathe(), lay_eggs(), and soar() to show the whole chain working.
